notes.front: What are Services without selectors?
notes.back: Services with no selector, paired with EndpointSlices you create, so they can front other backends, including ones outside the cluster.
notes.explanation: A normal Service finds Pods through its selector; a selectorless one relies on the EndpointSlices you supply.
notes.example: Like a switchboard extension that forwards to a number you type in by hand, rather than to whoever is at a given desk.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Service, “Services without selectors”
notes.evidence: Services most commonly abstract access to Kubernetes Pods thanks to the selector, but when used with a corresponding set of EndpointSlices objects and without a selector, the Service can abstract other kinds of backends, including ones that run outside the cluster.

notes.front: What are SRV records for named ports?
notes.back: DNS records created for each named port of a normal or headless Service, of the form _port-name._port-protocol.my-svc.my-namespace.svc.cluster-domain.example.
notes.explanation: For a regular Service they resolve to the port number and the Service's domain name.
notes.example: Like a phone book entry that gives not just the building but also the room number for "reception".
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, DNS for Services and Pods, “SRV records”
notes.evidence: SRV Records are created for named ports that are part of normal or headless services. For each named port, the SRV record has the form _port-name._port-protocol.my-svc.my-namespace.svc.cluster-domain.example .

notes.front: What is Pod dnsConfig?
notes.back: An optional Pod spec field that gives more control over the Pod's DNS settings, and works with any dnsPolicy.
notes.explanation: It is optional, except that a dnsPolicy of None requires it.
notes.example: Like writing your own address book for one phone instead of using the office directory.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, DNS for Services and Pods, “Pod's DNS Config”
notes.evidence: Pod's DNS Config allows users more control on the DNS settings for a Pod. The dnsConfig field is optional and it can work with any dnsPolicy settings.

notes.front: What is CoreDNS?
notes.back: A general-purpose authoritative DNS server that can serve as the cluster DNS.
notes.explanation: It is modular: plugins add its functions.
notes.example: Like a company switchboard that knows every internal extension and passes outside calls to the public network.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Customizing DNS Service, “CoreDNS”
notes.evidence: CoreDNS is a general-purpose authoritative DNS server that can serve as cluster DNS, complying with the DNS specifications . CoreDNS ConfigMap options CoreDNS is a DNS server that is modular and pluggable, with plugins adding new functionalities.

notes.front: What is the Corefile in the coredns ConfigMap?
notes.back: CoreDNS's configuration file, held as the Corefile key of the coredns ConfigMap in kube-system.
notes.explanation: Editing that ConfigMap is how a cluster administrator changes DNS service discovery.
notes.example: Like the rule book pinned to the switchboard, listing which calls go where.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Customizing DNS Service, “CoreDNS ConfigMap options”
notes.evidence: As a cluster administrator, you can modify the ConfigMap for the CoreDNS Corefile to change how DNS service discovery behaves for that cluster. In Kubernetes, CoreDNS is installed with the following default Corefile configuration: apiVersion : v1 kind : ConfigMap metadata : name : coredns namespace : kube-system

notes.front: What is --cluster-domain?
notes.back: The kubelet flag that sets the cluster's local DNS domain, such as cluster.local.
notes.explanation: DNS names need a domain; this flag supplies the local one that Service names end in.
notes.example: Like the company's internal email domain that every staff address ends in.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Customizing DNS Service, “Introduction”
notes.evidence: DNS names also need domains. You configure the local domain in the kubelet with the flag --cluster-domain=<default-local-domain> .

notes.front: Which components assign IP addresses to Pods, to Services and to Nodes?
notes.back: Pods: the network plugin. Services: kube-apiserver. Nodes: the kubelet or cloud-controller-manager.
notes.explanation: Each comes from a range configured in that component.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Cluster Networking, “Kubernetes IP address ranges”
notes.evidence: The network plugin is configured to assign IP addresses to Pods. The kube-apiserver is configured to assign IP addresses to Services. The kubelet or the cloud-controller-manager is configured to assign IP addresses to Nodes.

notes.front: May the IP ranges for Pods, Services and Nodes overlap?
notes.back: No. Clusters need non-overlapping addresses for Pods, Services and Nodes.
notes.explanation: Each range is configured separately, so you must keep them apart when you set them.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Cluster Networking, “Kubernetes IP address ranges”
notes.evidence: Kubernetes clusters require to allocate non-overlapping IP addresses for Pods, Services and Nodes, from a range of available addresses configured in the following components:

notes.front: In a kubeadm cluster, kubectl shows a Pod at 10.244.2.9 and a ClusterIP Service at 10.96.40.12. Which component gave the Service its address?
notes.back: B) kube-apiserver.
notes.choices:
A) The network plugin
B) kube-apiserver
C) kube-proxy
notes.choicesExplained: A: the network plugin assigns Pod addresses, such as 10.244.2.9. C: kube-proxy is not named among the components that assign addresses.
notes.explanation: Service addresses come from the range configured in kube-apiserver; Pod addresses from the network plugin.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Cluster Networking, “Kubernetes IP address ranges”
notes.evidence: The network plugin is configured to assign IP addresses to Pods. The kube-apiserver is configured to assign IP addresses to Services.

notes.front: What implements the Kubernetes network model on each node, and what do the common ones use to do it?
notes.back: The container runtime, most commonly using Container Network Interface (CNI) plugins.
notes.explanation: The runtime relies on these plugins for its network and security capabilities.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Cluster Networking, “How to implement the Kubernetes network model”
notes.evidence: The network model is implemented by the container runtime on each node. The most common container runtimes use Container Network Interface (CNI) plugins to manage their network and security capabilities.

notes.front: Of the four networking problems Kubernetes addresses, how is highly-coupled container-to-container communication solved?
notes.back: By Pods and localhost communications.
notes.explanation: Pod-to-Service and external-to-Service traffic are covered by Services instead.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Cluster Networking, “Cluster Networking”
notes.evidence: Highly-coupled container-to-container communications: this is solved by Pods and localhost communications. Pod-to-Pod communications: this is the primary focus of this document. Pod-to-Service communications: this is covered by Services .

notes.front: Do Pods in a cluster need address translation or host port mapping to reach each other?
notes.back: No. Every Pod has its own cluster-private IP, so all Pods can see each other without address translation.
notes.explanation: Containers in the same Pod reach each other's ports on localhost.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Connecting Applications with Services, “The Kubernetes model for connecting containers”
notes.evidence: Kubernetes gives every pod its own cluster-private IP address, so you do not need to explicitly create links between pods or map container ports to host ports. This means that containers within a Pod can all reach each other's ports on localhost, and all pods in a cluster can see each other without NAT.

notes.front: You are building a cluster and must give Pods their network interfaces and addresses. Which kind of component do most container runtimes use for this?
notes.back: C) A CNI plugin.
notes.choices:
A) A CSI driver
B) A device plugin
C) A CNI plugin
notes.choicesExplained: A: CSI drivers provide storage, not networking. B: device plugins advertise hardware such as GPUs.
notes.explanation: The most common runtimes use Container Network Interface plugins for network and security capabilities.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Cluster Networking, “How to implement the Kubernetes network model”
notes.evidence: The most common container runtimes use Container Network Interface (CNI) plugins to manage their network and security capabilities.

notes.front: Which imperative command creates a Service for an existing Deployment named web?
notes.back: kubectl expose deployment/web
notes.explanation: It is equivalent to applying a Service manifest whose selector matches the Deployment's Pods.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Connecting Applications with Services, “Creating a Service”
notes.evidence: kubectl expose deployment/my-nginx service/my-nginx exposed This is equivalent to kubectl apply -f in the following yaml:

notes.front: Which kubectl create subcommand makes a NodePort Service directly, without exposing a workload?
notes.back: kubectl create service nodeport <name>
notes.explanation: kubectl create service also has clusterip, externalname and loadbalancer subcommands.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, kubectl create, “See Also”
notes.evidence: kubectl create service clusterip kubectl create service externalname kubectl create service loadbalancer kubectl create service nodeport

notes.front: In a Service, what is the difference between port and targetPort?
notes.back: targetPort is the port the container accepts traffic on; port is the Service port other Pods use.
notes.explanation: The Service receives on port and forwards to targetPort on the selected Pods.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Connecting Applications with Services, “Creating a Service”
notes.evidence: targetPort : is the port the container accepts traffic on, port : is the abstracted Service port, which can be any port other pods use to access the Service

notes.front: If you leave targetPort out of a Service port, by default it is set to the same value as the {{c1::port}} field.
notes.back: port
notes.explanation: You only need targetPort when the container listens on a different port.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Service, “Port definitions”
notes.evidence: By default and for convenience, the `targetPort` is set to # the same value as the `port` field.

notes.front: By default, the control plane allocates a nodePort from the range {{c1::30000-32767}}.
notes.explanation: The range is a default, so a cluster can be configured with another.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Service, “type: NodePort”
notes.evidence: By default and for convenience, the Kubernetes control plane # will allocate a port from a range (default: 30000-32767)

notes.front: A NodePort Service has port 8080, targetPort 3000 and nodePort 31080. A client outside the cluster calls <node-IP>:31080. On which port does the container receive the traffic?
notes.choicesExplained: A: 31080 is the node's port, where outside traffic enters. B: 8080 is the Service port that other Pods use.
notes.explanation: targetPort is always the port the container accepts traffic on.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Connecting Applications with Services, “Creating a Service”
notes.evidence: targetPort : is the port the container accepts traffic on, port : is the abstracted Service port, which can be any port other pods use to access the Service

notes.front: Can a Service's targetPort refer to a port by name rather than number?
notes.back: Yes. Port definitions in Pods have names, and targetPort can reference them.
notes.explanation: The docs show a Service binding its targetPort to a named port in the Pod.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Service, “Port definitions”
notes.evidence: Port definitions in Pods have names, and you can reference these names in the targetPort attribute of a Service.

notes.front: The set of Pods targeted by a Service is usually determined by a {{c1::selector}} that you define.
notes.back: selector
notes.explanation: The docs say "usually": Services without selectors get their endpoints another way.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Service, “Defining a Service”
notes.evidence: The set of Pods targeted by a Service is usually determined by a selector that you define.

notes.front: For a Service without a selector, are its EndpointSlices created automatically?
notes.back: No. You map it to the backend's address and port by adding an EndpointSlice yourself.
notes.explanation: With no selector, there are no Pods for the control plane to find.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Service, “Services without selectors”
notes.evidence: Because this Service has no selector, the corresponding EndpointSlice objects are not created automatically. You can map the Service to the network address and port where it's running, by adding an EndpointSlice object manually.

notes.front: Apps in the cluster must reach a legacy database on a VM at 10.40.0.8:5432 through a Service called ledger-db. What do you create?
notes.back: B) A Service with no selector, plus an EndpointSlice pointing at 10.40.0.8:5432.
notes.choices:
A) A Service whose selector matches app=ledger-db
B) A Service with no selector, plus an EndpointSlice pointing at 10.40.0.8:5432
C) A Service with no selector and nothing else
notes.choicesExplained: A: a selector matches Pods, and the database is not a Pod. C: without a selector no EndpointSlices are created, so the Service would have no backends.
notes.explanation: Selectorless Services can abstract backends that run outside the cluster, using EndpointSlices you add.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Service, “Services without selectors”
notes.evidence: Because this Service has no selector, the corresponding EndpointSlice objects are not created automatically. You can map the Service to the network address and port where it's running, by adding an EndpointSlice object manually.

notes.front: How do you give a Service a cluster IP of your choosing, and what range must it be in?
notes.back: Set .spec.clusterIP; it must be a valid address within the API server's service-cluster-ip-range.
notes.explanation: The docs' reasons include reusing an existing DNS entry, or legacy systems tied to one IP address.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Service, “Choosing your own IP address”
notes.evidence: You can specify your own cluster IP address as part of a Service creation request. To do this, set the .spec.clusterIP field. For example, if you already have an existing DNS entry that you wish to reuse, or legacy systems that are configured for a specific IP address

notes.front: What does the API server return if you create a Service with an invalid clusterIP value?
notes.back: A 422 HTTP status code.
notes.explanation: The address must be valid IPv4 or IPv6 and inside the configured service-cluster-ip-range.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Service, “Choosing your own IP address”
notes.evidence: The IP address that you choose must be a valid IPv4 or IPv6 address from within the service-cluster-ip-range CIDR range that is configured for the API server. If you try to create a Service with an invalid clusterIP address value, the API server will return a 422 HTTP status code

notes.front: A payments backend must be reachable only by other workloads inside the cluster. You write the Service without a type field. Which type does it get, and does that fit?
notes.back: A) ClusterIP, which is the default and reachable only from within the cluster.
notes.choices:
A) ClusterIP: the default, reachable only from within the cluster
B) NodePort: the default, open on every node
C) LoadBalancer: the default on cloud providers
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: neither is the default type; both expose the Service outside the cluster.
notes.explanation: ClusterIP is used whenever a Service does not state a type.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Service, “Publishing Services (ServiceTypes)”
notes.evidence: ClusterIP Exposes the Service on a cluster-internal IP. Choosing this value makes the Service only reachable from within the cluster. This is the default that is used if you don't explicitly specify a type for a Service.

notes.front: Does a NodePort Service also get a cluster IP?
notes.back: Yes. To make the node port available, Kubernetes sets up a cluster IP as for type ClusterIP.
notes.explanation: The docs describe the types as nested: each level adds to the previous one, with one exception.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Service, “Publishing Services (ServiceTypes)”
notes.evidence: NodePort Exposes the Service on each Node's IP at a static port (the NodePort ). To make the node port available, Kubernetes sets up a cluster IP address, the same as if you had requested a Service of type: ClusterIP .

notes.front: You set a specific value in a Service's nodePort field. What does the control plane do, and whose job are port collisions?
notes.back: It either allocates that port or reports that the API transaction failed; avoiding collisions is up to you.
notes.explanation: The port must also be valid and inside the configured NodePort range.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Service, “Choosing your own port”
notes.evidence: If you want a specific port number, you can specify a value in the nodePort field. The control plane will either allocate you that port or report that the API transaction failed. This means that you need to take care of possible port collisions yourself.

notes.front: Does Kubernetes itself provide the load balancer for a Service of type LoadBalancer?
notes.back: No. You must provide one, or integrate the cluster with a cloud provider.
notes.explanation: The type asks for an external load balancer; something outside core Kubernetes has to supply it.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Service, “Publishing Services (ServiceTypes)”
notes.evidence: LoadBalancer Exposes the Service externally using an external load balancer. Kubernetes does not directly offer a load balancing component; you must provide one, or you can integrate your Kubernetes cluster with a cloud provider.

notes.front: On a kubeadm cluster in your own data centre, with no cloud integration and no load balancer add-on, you create a LoadBalancer Service. It never gets an external IP. Why?
notes.back: A) Nothing supplies a load balancer: Kubernetes does not offer one itself.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing supplies a load balancer: Kubernetes does not offer one itself
B) LoadBalancer Services need a selector on the node labels
C) kube-proxy is in iptables mode
notes.choicesExplained: B: a Service selector matches Pods, not nodes, and has nothing to do with getting an external address. C: kube-proxy's mode does not provide an external load balancer.
notes.explanation: You must provide a load balancer, or integrate the cluster with a cloud provider.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Service, “Publishing Services (ServiceTypes)”
notes.evidence: Kubernetes does not directly offer a load balancing component; you must provide one, or you can integrate your Kubernetes cluster with a cloud provider.

notes.front: Pods should reach a partner API at api.partner.example through the in-cluster name partner-api, using a DNS alias with no proxying. Which Service type fits?
notes.back: C) ExternalName
notes.choices:
A) ClusterIP
B) NodePort
C) ExternalName
notes.choicesExplained: A: ClusterIP gives an internal virtual IP in front of endpoints, not a DNS alias. B: NodePort opens a port on every node for incoming traffic.
notes.explanation: ExternalName makes the cluster DNS return an alias record for the external hostname, and sets up no proxying.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Service, “Publishing Services (ServiceTypes)”
notes.evidence: ExternalName Maps the Service to the contents of the externalName field (for example, to the hostname api.foo.bar.example ). The mapping configures your cluster's DNS server to return a CNAME record with that external hostname value. No proxying of any kind is set up.

notes.front: Which command lists the EndpointSlices of a Service named hostnames?
notes.back: kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=hostnames
notes.explanation: The ENDPOINTS column shows the Pod addresses the Service has found.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Debug Services, “Does the Service have any EndpointSlices?”
notes.evidence: kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name = hostnames NAME ADDRESSTYPE PORTS ENDPOINTS

notes.front: The Service checkout has selector app=checkout, but its EndpointSlice shows ENDPOINTS <none>. The Pods are Running with label app=check-out. What is wrong?
notes.back: A) The Service's selector does not match the Pods' labels.
notes.choices:
A) The selector does not match the Pods' labels
B) CoreDNS is down
C) The Service needs type NodePort
notes.choicesExplained: B: DNS resolves the Service name; it does not choose the Pods behind it. C: the type changes how the Service is exposed, not which Pods it selects.
notes.explanation: The docs name a typo in the selector or labels as a common mistake.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Debug Services, “Does the Service have any EndpointSlices?”
notes.evidence: If the ENDPOINTS column is <none> , you should check that the spec.selector field of your Service actually selects for metadata.labels values on your Pods. A common mistake is to have a typo or other error

notes.front: Since which Kubernetes version is the Endpoints API deprecated, and what replaces it?
notes.back: Deprecated since v1.33; EndpointSlice replaces it.
notes.explanation: So use kubectl get endpointslices where older guides use kubectl get endpoints.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, EndpointSlices, “EndpointSlice mirroring”
notes.evidence: Feature state: Deprecated since Kubernetes v1.33 The EndpointSlice API is a replacement for the older Endpoints API.

notes.front: For a Service without a selector, should you write Endpoints objects or EndpointSlices?
notes.back: EndpointSlices, created directly, rather than Endpoints left to be mirrored.
notes.explanation: Mirroring of Endpoints is deprecated along with the rest of the Endpoints API.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, EndpointSlices, “EndpointSlice mirroring”
notes.evidence: Users who manually specify endpoints for selectorless Services should do so by creating EndpointSlice resources directly, rather than by creating Endpoints resources and allowing them to be mirrored.

notes.front: Which label on an EndpointSlice lets you look up all the slices belonging to a Service?
notes.back: kubernetes.io/service-name
notes.explanation: That is why the debugging command filters with -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<service>.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, EndpointSlices, “Ownership”
notes.evidence: a kubernetes.io/service-name label that enables simple lookups of all EndpointSlices belonging to a Service.

notes.front: Which EndpointSlice condition says an endpoint is currently serving responses, and for a Pod maps to the Pod's Ready condition?
notes.back: serving
notes.explanation: An endpoint that is serving should be used as a target for Service traffic.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, EndpointSlices, “Conditions”
notes.evidence: The serving condition indicates that the endpoint is currently serving responses, and so it should be used as a target for Service traffic. For endpoints backed by a Pod, this maps to the Pod's Ready condition.

notes.front: Which EndpointSlice condition is set when the Pod behind an endpoint is first deleted?
notes.back: terminating
notes.explanation: It is set when the Pod receives a deletion timestamp.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, EndpointSlices, “Conditions”
notes.evidence: The terminating condition indicates that the endpoint is terminating. For endpoints backed by a Pod, this condition is set when the Pod is first deleted (that is, when it receives a deletion timestamp

notes.front: Which EndpointSlice condition is essentially a shortcut for "serving and not terminating"?
notes.back: ready
notes.explanation: It is also always true for Services with spec.publishNotReadyAddresses set to true.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, EndpointSlices, “Conditions”
notes.evidence: The ready condition is essentially a shortcut for checking " serving and not terminating "

notes.front: Pods were created before their Service. Why can't they find the Service through environment variables?
notes.back: The kubelet adds Service environment variables when a Pod starts, only for Services active then.
notes.explanation: Only Services active when the Pod runs get variables, which the docs call an ordering problem.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Connecting Applications with Services, “Environment Variables”
notes.evidence: When a Pod runs on a Node, the kubelet adds a set of environment variables for each active Service. This introduces an ordering problem.

notes.front: A normal (not headless) Service gets DNS address records of the form {{c1::my-svc.my-namespace.svc.cluster-domain.example}}, which resolve to its cluster IP.
notes.back: my-svc.my-namespace.svc.cluster-domain.example
notes.explanation: The cluster domain part is what --cluster-domain sets, often cluster.local.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, DNS for Services and Pods, “A/AAAA records”
notes.evidence: "Normal" (not headless) Services are assigned DNS A and/or AAAA records, depending on the IP family or families of the Service, with a name of the form my-svc.my-namespace.svc.cluster-domain.example . This resolves to the cluster IP of the Service.

notes.front: What does the DNS name of a headless Service resolve to, compared with a normal Service?
notes.back: The set of IPs of all the Pods it selects, not a single cluster IP.
notes.explanation: Clients are expected to use the whole set, or pick with round-robin.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, DNS for Services and Pods, “A/AAAA records”
notes.evidence: Headless Services (without a cluster IP) are also assigned DNS A and/or AAAA records, with a name of the form my-svc.my-namespace.svc.cluster-domain.example . Unlike normal Services, this resolves to the set of IPs of all of the Pods selected by the Service.

notes.front: A Pod in the staging namespace looks up billing, but the billing Service lives in the finance namespace. The lookup returns nothing. Which name should it use?
notes.back: B) billing.finance
notes.choices:
A) billing.staging
B) billing.finance
C) finance.billing
notes.choicesExplained: A: that asks for billing in the Pod's own namespace, where it does not exist. C: the Service name comes first, then its namespace.
notes.explanation: Queries without a namespace are limited to the Pod's own namespace.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, DNS for Services and Pods, “Namespaces of Services”
notes.evidence: DNS queries that don't specify a namespace are limited to the Pod's namespace. Access Services in other namespaces by specifying it in the DNS query.

notes.front: What does the SRV record of a named port resolve to for a regular Service, and for a headless one?
notes.back: Regular: the port number and the Service's domain name. Headless: one answer per backing Pod, with its port and domain name.
notes.explanation: The headless answers carry each Pod's name in the form hostname.my-svc.my-namespace.svc.cluster-domain.example.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, DNS for Services and Pods, “SRV records”
notes.evidence: For a regular Service, this resolves to the port number and the domain name: my-svc.my-namespace.svc.cluster-domain.example . For a headless Service, this resolves to multiple answers, one for each Pod that is backing the Service, and contains the port number and the domain name of the Pod

notes.front: A Pod in the default namespace has IP 172.17.0.3 and the cluster domain is cluster.local. What is its Pod DNS name?
notes.back: 172-17-0-3.default.pod.cluster.local
notes.explanation: The dots in the IP become dashes, followed by the namespace, pod and the cluster domain.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, DNS for Services and Pods, “Pods”
notes.evidence: For example, if a Pod in the default namespace has the IP address 172.17.0.3, and the domain name for your cluster is cluster.local , then the Pod has a DNS name: 172-17-0-3.default.pod.cluster.local

notes.front: Under which dnsPolicy is any query that does not match the cluster domain suffix forwarded to an upstream nameserver?
notes.back: ClusterFirst
notes.explanation: Names in the cluster domain are answered by the cluster DNS; everything else goes upstream.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, DNS for Services and Pods, “Pod's DNS Policy”
notes.evidence: " ClusterFirst ": Any DNS query that does not match the configured cluster domain suffix, such as " www.kubernetes.io ", is forwarded to an upstream nameserver by the DNS server.

notes.front: Under which dnsPolicy does a Pod inherit its name resolution configuration from the node it runs on?
notes.back: Default
notes.explanation: Despite its name, it is not the policy used when none is set.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, DNS for Services and Pods, “Pod's DNS Policy”
notes.evidence: " Default ": The Pod inherits the name resolution configuration from the node that the Pods run on.

notes.front: Which dnsPolicy should you set explicitly for a Pod running with hostNetwork?
notes.back: ClusterFirstWithHostNet
notes.explanation: Otherwise a hostNetwork Pod with ClusterFirst falls back to the behaviour of the Default policy.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, DNS for Services and Pods, “Pod's DNS Policy”
notes.evidence: For Pods running with hostNetwork, you should explicitly set its DNS policy to " ClusterFirstWithHostNet ". Otherwise, Pods running with hostNetwork and "ClusterFirst" will fallback to the behavior of the "Default" policy.

notes.front: Which dnsPolicy lets a Pod ignore the DNS settings from the Kubernetes environment, taking all of them from dnsConfig?
notes.back: None
notes.explanation: That is why dnsConfig becomes mandatory with this policy.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, DNS for Services and Pods, “Pod's DNS Policy”
notes.evidence: " None ": It allows a Pod to ignore DNS settings from the Kubernetes environment. All DNS settings are supposed to be provided using the dnsConfig field in the Pod Spec.

notes.front: A Pod spec sets no dnsPolicy at all. Which policy does the Pod get?
notes.back: B) ClusterFirst
notes.choices:
A) Default
B) ClusterFirst
C) None
notes.choicesExplained: A: "Default" is not the default DNS policy; it means inherit from the node. C: None needs a dnsConfig and must be set on purpose.
notes.explanation: The docs warn that the policy named Default is not the one used when dnsPolicy is left out.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, DNS for Services and Pods, “Pod's DNS Policy”
notes.evidence: Note: "Default" is not the default DNS policy. If dnsPolicy is not explicitly specified, then "ClusterFirst" is used.

notes.front: When must a Pod specify the dnsConfig field?
notes.back: When its dnsPolicy is set to None.
notes.explanation: For every other policy the field is optional.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, DNS for Services and Pods, “Pod's DNS Config”
notes.evidence: However, when a Pod's dnsPolicy is set to " None ", the dnsConfig field has to be specified.

notes.front: In dnsConfig, how many nameservers may you list, and when must there be at least one?
notes.back: At most 3; at least one when dnsPolicy is None.
notes.explanation: The servers listed are combined with the base nameservers from the chosen policy.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, DNS for Services and Pods, “Pod's DNS Config”
notes.evidence: nameservers : a list of IP addresses that will be used as DNS servers for the Pod. There can be at most 3 IP addresses specified. When the Pod's dnsPolicy is set to " None ", the list must contain at least one IP address

notes.front: The CoreDNS Service is named {{c1::kube-dns}} in the metadata.name field.
notes.back: kube-dns
notes.explanation: The docs say the old name is kept for interoperability with workloads that relied on the legacy kube-dns Service name.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Customizing DNS Service, “CoreDNS”
notes.evidence: The CoreDNS Service is named kube-dns in the metadata.name field. The intent is to ensure greater interoperability with workloads that relied on the legacy kube-dns Service name to resolve addresses internal to the cluster.

notes.front: You want to confirm the cluster DNS Service is running, and kubectl get svc coredns -n kube-system returns NotFound. What should you run instead?
notes.back: A) kubectl get services kube-dns --namespace=kube-system
notes.choices:
A) kubectl get services kube-dns --namespace=kube-system
B) kubectl get services coredns --namespace=default
C) kubectl get services dns --all-namespaces
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Service lives in kube-system and is not called coredns. C: its name is kube-dns, not dns.
notes.explanation: CoreDNS keeps the legacy Service name kube-dns.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Connecting Applications with Services, “DNS”
notes.evidence: You can check if it's running on your cluster: kubectl get services kube-dns --namespace = kube-system

notes.front: How does each container learn the IP address of the cluster DNS server?
notes.back: The kubelet passes it, set with its --cluster-dns=<dns-service-ip> flag.
notes.explanation: CoreDNS run as a Deployment is typically exposed as a Service with a static IP address.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Customizing DNS Service, “CoreDNS”
notes.evidence: If you are running CoreDNS as a Deployment, it will typically be exposed as a Kubernetes Service with a static IP address. The kubelet passes DNS resolver information to each container with the --cluster-dns=<dns-service-ip> flag.

notes.front: Which plugin in the default Corefile makes CoreDNS reply to DNS queries based on the IPs of Services and Pods?
notes.back: kubernetes
notes.explanation: In the default Corefile it serves cluster.local and the reverse-lookup zones.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Customizing DNS Service, “CoreDNS ConfigMap options”
notes.evidence: kubernetes : CoreDNS will reply to DNS queries based on IP of the Services and Pods.

notes.front: Which plugin in the default Corefile sends queries outside the cluster domain to the resolvers in /etc/resolv.conf?
notes.back: forward
notes.explanation: Changing its target is how you point non-cluster lookups at another nameserver.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Customizing DNS Service, “CoreDNS ConfigMap options”
notes.evidence: forward : Any queries that are not within the Kubernetes cluster domain are forwarded to predefined resolvers (/etc/resolv.conf).

notes.front: Which plugin in the default Corefile enables a frontend cache?
notes.back: cache
notes.explanation: The default Corefile sets it as cache 30.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Customizing DNS Service, “CoreDNS ConfigMap options”
notes.evidence: cache : This enables a frontend cache.

notes.front: Which plugin in the default Corefile detects simple forwarding loops and halts CoreDNS if it finds one?
notes.back: loop
notes.explanation: It stops the CoreDNS process rather than let a loop run on.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Customizing DNS Service, “CoreDNS ConfigMap options”
notes.evidence: loop : Detects simple forwarding loops and halts the CoreDNS process if a loop is found.

notes.front: Which plugin in the default Corefile reloads a changed Corefile automatically, and how long should you allow?
notes.back: reload; allow two minutes after editing the ConfigMap.
notes.explanation: Edits to the coredns ConfigMap are picked up by this plugin after a short wait.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Customizing DNS Service, “CoreDNS ConfigMap options”
notes.evidence: reload : Allows automatic reload of a changed Corefile. After you edit the ConfigMap configuration, allow two minutes for your changes to take effect.

notes.front: Names ending in corp.internal must be resolved by your company DNS server at 10.20.0.53, while all other lookups stay as they are. What do you add to the Corefile?
notes.back: B) A separate server block: corp.internal:53 { errors cache 30 forward . 10.20.0.53 }
notes.choicesExplained: A: that sends all non-cluster lookups to the company server, not just corp.internal. C: dnsConfig is set per Pod; the stub domain belongs in the cluster DNS configuration.
notes.explanation: A stanza for the domain in the CoreDNS ConfigMap forwards just that domain.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Customizing DNS Service, “Configuration of Stub-domain and upstream nameserver using CoreDNS”
notes.evidence: To configure it in CoreDNS, the cluster administrator creates the following stanza in the CoreDNS ConfigMap. consul.local:53 { errors cache 30 forward . 10.150.0.1 }

notes.front: How do you force all non-cluster DNS lookups through one upstream nameserver?
notes.back: Point the forward plugin at that nameserver instead of /etc/resolv.conf, e.g. forward . 172.16.0.1
notes.explanation: The forward line in the main server block controls where non-cluster queries go.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Customizing DNS Service, “Configuration of Stub-domain and upstream nameserver using CoreDNS”
notes.evidence: To explicitly force all non-cluster DNS lookups to go through a specific nameserver at 172.16.0.1, point the forward to the nameserver instead of /etc/resolv.conf forward . 172.16.0.1

notes.front: kube-proxy's log says "Using iptables Proxier". Which mode is it in, and what is the most common other mode?
notes.back: iptables mode; the most common other mode is ipvs.
notes.explanation: kube-proxy is the default implementation of Services, used on most clusters.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Debug Services, “Is the kube-proxy working?”
notes.evidence: the line Using iptables Proxier indicates that kube-proxy is running in "iptables" mode. The most common other mode is "ipvs".
